patch.meaning: hotter than all the others

en:card:a1p10l2/hottest.reason: "More hot" models a wrong comparative form for A1 learners, so the gloss should use "hotter".

patch.example: There is a lot of snow on the mountains.

en:card:a1p10l2/snow.reason: The gloss defines the noun, but the example uses the verb ("it will snow").

patch.meaning: very hard and unpleasant, like bad weather

en:card:a1p10l3/harsh.reason: "Harsh" means severe and unpleasant, not specifically cold, so the gloss is too narrow; the word is also above A1. / 'Harsh' means severe and unpleasant, not specifically cold.

patch.example: This shirt costs twenty pounds.

en:card:a1p11l1/twenty.reason: A British English course should use pounds in its money examples.

patch.example: I'd like to withdraw some money from the cash machine.

en:card:a1p11l1/withdraw.reason: "From the machine" is vague; "cash machine" is the natural British term.

patch.meaning: a small plastic thing you pay with

en:card:a1p11l3/card.reason: The gloss "a plastic way to pay" is awkward and vague; a card is an object, not a 'way'. / A card is not 'a way' to pay, so 'a plastic way to pay' is awkward; it is better described as a plastic object.

patch.example: Could I have a receipt, please?

en:card:a1p11l3/receipt.reason: 'Could I get' is US-leaning and 'purchase' is formal for A1; 'Could I have a receipt, please?' is the natural British request.

patch.example: I have two ten-pound notes in my wallet.

en:card:a1p11l4/notes.reason: The example does not show that 'notes' means money, and a learner could read it as written notes.

patch.example: The amount on the bill is twenty pounds.

en:card:a1p11l5/amount.reason: 'Paid the amount in full' is a formal phrase above A1, and a simpler example shows the meaning better.

patch.example: I have enough money for a coffee.

en:card:a1p11l5/enough.reason: 'Saved enough money for college' is a US idiom, and a simple everyday example suits a British A1 lesson better.

patch.example: There is a big sale at the shop this week.

en:card:a1p11l5/sale.reason: In British English "on sale" means 'available to buy', which contradicts the gloss about lower prices; the British form is "in the sale", or the noun used on its own.

patch.meaning: a person who helps people with legal problems

en:card:a1p12l2/lawyer.reason: 'Works with the law' also fits judges and police officers, so it does not define a lawyer. / 'Works with the law' also fits judges and police officers.

patch.example: The shopkeeper opens the shop at nine.

en:card:a1p12l3/shopkeeper.reason: 'The shopkeeper opens at nine' is a colloquial shortcut; at A1 the clearer form names what is opened.

patch.example: The midwife helped my sister when her baby was born.

en:card:a1p12l5/midwife.reason: The gloss is fine, but "helped the baby arrive" is an awkward way to describe a midwife's work.

patch.example: A bird is singing in the tree.

en:card:a1p13l2/bird.reason: The present simple 'A bird sings in the tree' sounds odd for a single scene; the present continuous is more natural.

patch.meaning: a water animal with a hard shell
patch.example: The turtle swims slowly in the sea.

en:card:a1p13l3/turtle.reason: In British English a turtle lives in or near water, but the gloss and the walking example describe a tortoise. / In British English a turtle lives in water and a slow walker on land is a tortoise, so both the gloss and the example point to the wrong animal.

patch.example: We play football in the afternoon.

en:card:a1p14l1/afternoon.reason: Lunch is usually eaten around midday, so 'We eat lunch in the afternoon' is an odd example and clashes with the gloss.

patch.example: Christmas is in December.

en:card:a1p14l1/december.reason: 'In the month of December' is wordy; a native speaker would simply say 'in December'.

patch.example: I go back to school on Monday.

en:card:a1p14l1/monday.reason: The example only repeats the gloss word for word, so it does not show the word in natural use.

patch.example: My birthday is in July.

en:card:a1p14l2/july.reason: "in the month of July" is wordy and unnatural for a simple statement; a native speaker would just say "in July".

patch.example: My birthday is in June.

en:card:a1p14l4/june.reason: The example only repeats the gloss instead of showing the word in natural use.

patch.meaning: twelve o'clock in the middle of the day

en:card:a1p14l5/noon.reason: "twelve o'clock in the day" is a slightly odd gloss; "in the middle of the day" is clearer and more natural.

patch.example: We have an English class on Wednesday.

en:card:a1p14l5/wednesday.reason: In a Monday-to-Sunday week, 'the middle day of the week' is debatable, so a plain everyday example is safer.

patch.example: We often relax at the weekend.

en:card:a1p14l5/weekend.reason: "on the weekend" is American; British English uses "at the weekend", and the card example models usage for learners.

patch.example: Draw a square on the paper.

en:card:a1p15l1/square.reason: 'The window is a square' is an unnatural use of the noun, since a window is usually described as square, not as 'a square'. / The example repeats the gloss and sounds redundant rather than natural.

patch.meaning: normal; not very big and not very small

en:card:a1p15l5/average.reason: 'Not big or small' is ambiguous for learners; 'not very big and not very small' says clearly that it is in the middle.

patch.meaning: a round shape with a pointed top

en:card:a1p15l5/cone.reason: The gloss lists features without saying what a cone is; it should read as a noun phrase naming a shape. / The gloss lists features without saying what a cone is, so it does not read as a definition.

patch.meaning: has; used in "takes a shower"

en:card:a1p16l1/takes.reason: The infinitive gloss 'to have' does not match the inflected term 'takes', unlike the other inflected cards.

patch.meaning: makes food ready to eat, often by heating

en:card:a1p16l2/cooks.reason: 'Makes food hot' is inaccurate because heating leftovers is not cooking; cooking means preparing food, usually with heat. / Cooking means preparing food, not just making it hot, so the gloss needs to say that within eight words.

patch.example: He glances at his phone before bed.

en:card:a1p16l3/glances at.reason: The gloss is fine and the term is set by the lesson, but 'before sleeping' is unnatural; 'before bed' is the natural, simpler phrase.

patch.meaning: to look at words and understand them

en:card:a1p16l3/read.reason: The gloss is missing its object ("understand them"), so it reads as ungrammatical.

patch.example: He works out at the gym every day.

en:card:a1p16l4/works out.reason: "Daily" at the end of the sentence sounds stiff; "every day" is the natural A1 phrasing.

patch.meaning: to pick what you want from several things

en:card:a1p16l5/choose.reason: "To pick one thing" clashes with the example, where several clothes are chosen; choosing means picking from several options.

patch.meaning: to get an alarm clock ready to ring
patch.example: I always set my alarm before I go to bed.

en:card:a1p16l5/set.reason: "Before I sleep" sounds slightly off; "before I go to bed" is the natural phrase, and the gloss reads better with "alarm clock".

patch.meaning: a set of printed pages that you read
patch.example: Open your book at page ten.

en:card:a1p17l1/book.reason: British classroom usage is "open your book at page ten", and "pages of words to read" is a clumsy gloss.

patch.meaning: a sheet of paper with questions to answer

en:card:a1p17l2/worksheet.reason: "A paper with questions" is unidiomatic; "a sheet of paper" is the natural phrasing.

patch.meaning: a metal object that rings

en:card:a1p17l3/bell.reason: A school bell signals when lessons start and end rather than telling the time, so the gloss is misleading. / A bell signals something rather than telling the time, so the gloss is misleading.

patch.example: I need to sharpen my pencil before the test.

en:card:a1p17l4/sharpen.reason: Sharpening makes a pencil shorter, so 'it's too short' is an illogical reason; the comma splice also needs fixing.

patch.meaning: a lamp, or brightness that helps you see

en:card:a1p18l1/light.reason: 'What lets you see in the dark' is an odd definition, and the example uses 'light' to mean a lamp. / The example uses 'light' as a lamp, but the gloss only describes light in the dark, so it does not match the example.

patch.meaning: a soft thing for your head in bed

en:card:a1p18l1/pillow.reason: Calling a pillow "a soft bag for your head" is an odd, misleading description. / A pillow is not a bag, so the gloss is slightly misleading.

patch.meaning: paid straight from your bank account

en:card:a1p19l2/debit.reason: The term 'debit' is not itself a card, so the gloss should point to the chunk 'debit card'. / The term 'debit' is used as a modifier in 'debit card', so the gloss should describe 'debit', not the card.

patch.meaning: a person you pay at the checkout

en:card:a1p19l3/cashier.reason: "A person who takes your money" could describe a thief, so the gloss needs the shop context.

patch.meaning: small amounts of food you eat between meals

en:card:a1p19l3/snacks.reason: 'Small food between meals' is awkward English for a plural noun and is not a clear gloss.

patch.example: There is a big discount on cheese this week.

en:card:a1p19l4/discount.reason: "This shop has a big discount" is slightly unnatural, because a discount is normally on a particular product.

patch.meaning: the place in a shop where you pay

en:card:a1p19l4/till.reason: The gloss describes only the cash drawer, but the example 'the queue at the till' uses the place where you pay.

patch.meaning: more than one person

en:card:a1p1l1/people.reason: 'Many men and women' wrongly suggests that 'people' excludes children; 'more than one person' is the true gloss.

patch.example: The mice live under the floor.

en:card:a1p1l2/mice.reason: "In the story" refers to a story the learner has never seen, so the example sounds odd out of context.

patch.example: The men came to the party with their wives.

en:card:a1p1l3/wives.reason: "Both wives" with no owner sounds as if one man has two wives, which is odd and confusing.

patch.meaning: plural of "life"; the state of being alive

en:card:a1p1l5/lives.reason: The gloss describes a length of time, but in "save lives" the word means people's existence (being alive), so the gloss and the example do not match.

patch.example: I usually walk to work because it's not far.

en:card:a1p20l2/walk.reason: The example is a comma splice, which is poor punctuation to model for learners.

patch.example: We saw a jet flying high in the sky.

en:card:a1p20l3/jet.reason: 'The jet is the fastest way to travel abroad' is a stilted generalisation, not a natural use of the word.

patch.meaning: metal things that open doors or start cars

en:card:a1p20l3/keys.reason: 'Metal things that start a car' is vague and too narrow for 'keys', which also open doors. / The gloss is too narrow, because keys also open doors.

patch.meaning: a safety strap in a car or plane

en:card:a1p20l3/seatbelt.reason: The gloss could describe many straps; it should say it is worn in a car or plane. / The gloss is too vague to identify a seatbelt; naming where it is used makes it a true definition.

patch.meaning: a longer way when a road is closed

en:card:a1p20l4/detour.reason: 'A longer way around a problem' is abstract; a concrete road gloss suits A1 and matches the example. / 'A longer way around a problem' is abstract for A1; a concrete road-based gloss is clearer, and the term itself cannot be swapped here.

patch.example: He wears a scarf round his neck.

en:card:a1p21l3/neck.reason: A scarf is worn 'round/around' the neck, not 'on' it, so the example teaches an unnatural preposition.

patch.example: My wrists hurt after typing all day.
patch.meaning: the joints where your hands join your arms

en:card:a1p21l5/wrists.reason: The term is plural 'wrists' but the example uses the singular 'wrist'. / "Thin parts" is imprecise; wrists are the joints between the hands and the arms.

patch.meaning: small paper squares you stick on letters

en:card:a1p22l2/stamps.reason: The gloss does not say what stamps are for. / The gloss does not say that stamps are stuck on letters for posting.

patch.meaning: moving in time with music that is playing

en:card:a1p22l2/to music.reason: 'Following the sound of a song' does not explain the phrase 'to music' as used in 'dance to music'.

patch.meaning: outside, not in a building
patch.example: The children like to play outdoors.

en:card:a1p22l3/outdoors.reason: "Not in a house" is too narrow, since outdoors means not in any building, and "camp outdoors" is redundant.

patch.meaning: words that tell about people and events

en:card:a1p22l3/stories.reason: The gloss uses "tales", which is harder than the A1 word it explains. / 'tales' is a harder word than 'stories' for an A1 learner.

patch.meaning: riding a bicycle

en:card:a1p22l4/on a bike.reason: In the example, "on a bike" means travelling by bicycle, so "sitting on a bicycle" misdescribes it.

patch.meaning: a language you are starting to learn

en:card:a1p22l5/a new language.reason: The gloss 'words and rules you have not learned' is an odd, inaccurate definition of a language that is new to you.

patch.meaning: the verb be, used with he, she, it

en:card:a1p2l2/is.reason: The gloss suggests that "is" itself means weather; it should say that here it is used with "it" to talk about the weather. / The verb 'is' does not mean weather; the gloss should give its grammar use, not the topic of the example.

patch.meaning: starts a question with you, we or they

en:card:a1p2l3/are.reason: "Are" also starts questions with "we" and "they", so the gloss is incomplete.

patch.meaning: starts a question with he, she or it

en:card:a1p2l3/does.reason: "Does" is also used with "it", so the gloss is incomplete.

patch.meaning: to eat or drink something

en:card:a1p2l4/have.reason: "Drink a meal" is not natural English, so the gloss needs rewording. / "Drink a meal" is unnatural; the gloss should cover eating or drinking something.

patch.example: Birds fly south for the winter.

en:card:a1p2l5/fly.reason: Birds fly south before winter, so "for the winter" is the natural and accurate phrase.

patch.example: His family is poor, so they can't buy new clothes.

en:card:a1p3l4/poor.reason: In "The poor man", "poor" before a noun often means 'unlucky, pitiable', so the example does not clearly show the meaning 'having little money'.

patch.example: He was the last person to arrive.

en:card:a1p3l5/last.reason: "He was the last person here" is vague; a verb such as "to arrive" shows clearly that he came after all the others.

patch.meaning: used with the weekend, Christmas and Easter

en:card:a1p4l2/at.reason: British English says "in the holidays" or "on holiday", not "at holidays", so the gloss teaches a false rule. / 'At the holidays' is US usage; British English says 'at the weekend', 'at Christmas' and 'at Easter'.

patch.example: I make breakfast every morning.

en:card:a1p5l1/make.reason: 'Everyone can make a mistake' is slightly unnatural (natives say 'Everyone makes mistakes'), and it shows a fixed phrase rather than the 'create' sense in the gloss.

patch.meaning: used in "how far" to ask about distance

en:card:a1p6l4/how.reason: "To ask distance" is slightly ungrammatical; natural English is "to ask about distance".

patch.meaning: asks about a thing or information

en:card:a1p6l5/what.reason: "Or problem" is an odd gloss for "what", which asks about things or information in general, not problems specifically.

patch.meaning: a girl or woman with the same parents

en:card:a1p7l1/sister.reason: 'A girl with the same parents' leaves out adult sisters and does not say whose parents. / A sister can be an adult, so 'a girl' alone is too narrow.

patch.meaning: the woman someone is married to

en:card:a1p7l1/wife.reason: 'A woman who is married' defines a married woman, not the relationship shown in 'His wife'.

patch.meaning: a woman who acts in films or plays

en:card:a1p7l3/actress.reason: The gloss limits actresses to films, but the word also covers stage and TV acting. / An actress also acts in plays and on TV, so "films" alone is too narrow.

patch.meaning: a woman chosen to help guide a child

en:card:a1p7l4/godmother.reason: 'A special woman friend of a child's family' does not say what a godmother actually is. / 'A special woman friend of the family' misses the real meaning of a godmother.

patch.meaning: the wife of a duke

en:card:a1p7l5/duchess.reason: 'A very high title' is vague, and the gloss should give the actual rank and its link to a duke. / 'A very high title' is vague; 'the wife of a duke' is a clearer, true gloss.

patch.meaning: a hot brown drink made from roasted beans

en:card:a1p8l1/coffee.reason: 'A hot brown drink' also describes tea, so the gloss does not identify coffee.

patch.example: Could we see the menu, please?

en:card:a1p8l2/menu.reason: "Can we get the menu for the table?" is an odd way to ask; a learner needs the standard restaurant request.

patch.example: Can I have a slice of cake, please?

en:card:a1p8l3/slice.reason: Ordering a single slice of pizza "to share" is an odd scenario.

patch.meaning: very dark; coffee or tea with no milk
patch.example: I like my coffee black.

en:card:a1p8l4/black.reason: The gloss says tea with no milk, but "black tea to green tea" uses the tea-variety sense, so the example contradicts the gloss. / The example uses 'black tea' as a tea variety, which contradicts the 'no milk' sense in the gloss.

patch.meaning: US word for the bill in a restaurant
patch.example: In New York, we asked for the check.

en:card:a1p8l4/check.reason: "Check" for the bill is US-only, and the example "the bill, or the check?" is unnatural, so the card should label it as American. / 'Check' for a restaurant bill is US English, and the example awkwardly offers both words.

patch.meaning: the flesh of animals, eaten as food
patch.example: She's a vegetarian, so she doesn't eat meat.

en:card:a1p8l4/meat.reason: "Food that comes from animals" also covers milk and eggs, and the clipped example "so no meat for her" is not a model sentence. / "Food that comes from animals" also covers eggs and milk, so the gloss is not true as written.

patch.meaning: a thick, flat piece of beef

en:card:a1p8l4/steak.reason: Steak is not necessarily cooked; raw steak is still steak, so the gloss is slightly false.

patch.meaning: not sparkling; with no bubbles

en:card:a1p8l5/still.reason: "Still" is an adjective, but the gloss defines it as if it were a noun meaning water. / "Still" is an adjective here, but the gloss reads like a noun phrase; it should describe the quality.

patch.meaning: a long, warm jacket you wear outside

en:card:a1p9l1/coat.reason: "Warm clothing you wear outside" also fits a scarf or a jumper, so the gloss does not pick out a coat.

patch.meaning: trousers made of strong cotton, often blue

en:card:a1p9l1/jeans.reason: Jeans are not always blue, so the gloss is too narrow.

patch.meaning: a top with a collar and buttons

en:card:a1p9l2/shirt.reason: "Clothing for the top of your body" also covers a T-shirt, a jumper or a coat, so it does not define a shirt.

patch.meaning: a warm top with long sleeves

en:card:a1p9l3/sweater.reason: "Sweater" is common in British English too, but the gloss wrongly says it is always made of wool. / Sweaters are not always wool; 'sweater' itself is also used in British English, so the term can stay.

patch.example: He put on his trainers and went for a run.

en:card:a1p9l5/trainers.reason: "Before the run" sounds odd with no run mentioned earlier; "went for a run" is more natural.

patch.example: That was the worst film I've ever seen.

en:card:a2p10l2/worst.reason: After a superlative, natural English uses "I've ever seen", not the past simple "I saw".

patch.example: He is the funniest boy in our class.

en:card:a2p10l4/funniest.reason: "In class" without a determiner sounds American; British English prefers "in our class" here.

patch.meaning: without meat, or not eating meat

en:card:a2p11l2/vegetarian.reason: The gloss "not eating meat" describes a person, but the example uses the word for dishes, so the gloss should cover food without meat.

patch.example: Could I have some tap water as well?

en:card:a2p11l2/water.reason: "Could I get" is a US-leaning request form; British restaurant usage is "Could I have".

patch.meaning: an informal word for children
patch.example: Is there a kids' menu, please?

en:card:a2p11l3/kids.reason: The example is redundant and lacks the apostrophe, and "young people" over-widens the gloss. / The gloss is too broad and the example repeats itself ('kids menu for the children').

patch.meaning: cooked between rare and well done
patch.example: I'd like my steak medium, please.

en:card:a2p11l3/medium.reason: The gloss is clumsy, and "not too well done" in the example is awkward.

patch.example: Could we have some extra ketchup with our chips, please?

en:card:a2p11l4/ketchup.reason: The card uses US 'fries' and 'Could we get'; the British forms are 'chips' and 'Could we have'.

patch.example: The meal was excellent. Please thank the chef.

en:card:a2p11l4/meal.reason: The example has a comma splice, and "excellent tonight" is slightly awkward.

patch.example: We booked a table for eight o'clock.

en:card:a2p11l5/booked.reason: The example is illogical (a fully booked restaurant has no free tables, so waiting outside makes little sense), and it uses "fully booked" rather than the gloss meaning "reserved ahead".

patch.example: Could we have a doggy bag for the rest, please?

en:card:a2p11l5/doggy.reason: The example is a comma splice ending in a question mark, and 'box this up' sounds American; a simple, natural British request works better.

patch.meaning: usually; in the usual way

en:card:a2p12l1/normally.reason: The gloss "in most normal situations" is circular because it defines the word with "normal".

patch.meaning: on some occasions, but not always

en:card:a2p12l2/sometimes.reason: "On some days" ties the meaning to days, but "sometimes" refers to any occasion.

patch.meaning: sometimes, but not often

en:card:a2p12l3/once in a while.reason: "A few times a year" is a false, over-specific frequency; "once in a while" just means occasionally.

patch.meaning: in "next to": beside, very close to

en:card:a2p13l1/next.reason: "Next" alone does not mean "beside", so the gloss should make clear the meaning belongs to the phrase "next to".

patch.example: The supermarket is opposite the bakery.

en:card:a2p13l1/opposite.reason: British English uses "opposite the bakery", not "opposite from", so the example teaches a wrong collocation.

patch.example: Go straight on at the traffic lights.

en:card:a2p13l1/straight.reason: In British directions the natural phrase is "go straight on", so the example sounds clipped without "on".

patch.meaning: on the other side of a corner

en:card:a2p13l2/around.reason: Glossing "around" as "past" is misleading, because in "around the corner" it means on the other side of the corner. / 'past' is a misleading gloss for 'around the corner'.

patch.example: Walk for five minutes and you'll see it.

en:card:a2p13l2/for.reason: "Two blocks" is American; a British learner would hear a time or distance instead.

patch.meaning: a wide way for cars and other traffic

en:card:a2p13l2/road.reason: "A hard path for cars" is an odd, unnatural definition of "road".

patch.example: You can't miss it. It's in the town square.

en:card:a2p13l5/in.reason: The example joins two sentences with a comma, which is a comma splice; a full stop is better for a model sentence.

patch.example: The nearest cash machine is just inside the station.

en:card:a2p13l5/inside.reason: "ATM" is the US-leaning term (British English says "cash machine"), and "just inside" reads more naturally.

patch.meaning: at a place, as in "on the corner"
patch.example: Turn left and the bank is on the corner.

en:card:a2p13l5/on.reason: "Touching a place" is an unclear gloss for "on the corner", and the example contains a comma splice.

patch.example: Let's meet at the cinema at seven.

en:card:a2p14l1/meet.reason: The example uses the phrasal verb "meet up" instead of the bare term "meet" that the card teaches.

patch.meaning: to decide something is a certain thing
patch.example: It's late, so let's call it a day.

en:card:a2p14l2/call.reason: 'Call it a rain check' is not a real idiom (the US phrase is 'take a rain check'), and the example does not show the glossed sense of 'call it'. / 'Rain check' is a US idiom, too hard for A2, and the gloss does not match its sense.

patch.example: Let's arrange to meet for coffee next week.

en:card:a2p14l3/arrange.reason: 'Arrange for coffee' is unnatural, because 'arrange' needs an object or 'to + verb'.

patch.meaning: deciding or intending to do something

en:card:a2p14l3/planning.reason: In 'planning to have a picnic', the verb means intending or deciding, not getting ready.

patch.meaning: to hold a time free for something
patch.example: Please keep Thursday evening free for the party.

en:card:a2p14l4/keep.reason: 'Keep it for Thursday' is not natural; the usual phrase is 'keep a time free'. / 'Keep it for Thursday' is unnatural; 'keep Thursday free' is the normal collocation.

patch.example: I'll write a quick message to confirm the time.

en:card:a2p14l4/write.reason: 'Write you a text' is unnatural in British English, where people 'send a text' or 'text you'.

patch.meaning: to decide something together

en:card:a2p14l5/agree.reason: "To say yes to the same idea" is an awkward, vague gloss and does not match the example, where "agree on" means deciding something together.

patch.example: I'd like to withdraw fifty pounds from my account, please.

en:card:a2p15l1/withdraw.reason: Asking "Could I withdraw some cash from the machine?" sounds like asking permission and is unnatural; a counter request reads better.

patch.example: I'd like to send this by airmail, please.

en:card:a2p15l3/airmail.reason: 'By airmail post' is redundant; people simply say 'by airmail'.

patch.example: My card was declined, so I paid in cash.

en:card:a2p15l3/declined.reason: "Declined by the machine" is an odd collocation; people simply say a card was declined.

patch.example: I've forgotten the PIN for my bank card.

en:card:a2p15l4/pin.reason: The gloss says a PIN is for your bank card but the example ties it to the account, and British English prefers the present perfect "I've forgotten".

patch.example: Could you tell me the cost of sending this parcel?

en:card:a2p15l5/cost.reason: "the cost to send" is less natural than "the cost of sending" in British English.

patch.meaning: goods or a parcel sent to you

en:card:a2p15l5/delivery.reason: The gloss says 'brought to your home' but the example has the learner collecting it from the post office, so the gloss should be broader. / The gloss says 'to your home' but the example collects the delivery from the post office.

patch.meaning: to replace something old or expired

en:card:a2p15l5/renew.reason: To renew a card means to get a new one because the old one has expired, not just 'a new copy', which suggests a duplicate. / 'Get a new copy' misses the idea of replacing something that has expired.

patch.example: I always buy my bread from the local bakery.

en:card:a2p16l2/local.reason: "My area has lots of local shops" is redundant and unnatural, since shops in your area are by definition local.

patch.example: I live in a quiet residential area.
